title: Senate Clears 60-Vote Hurdle on College Sports Bill; Lobbying War Intensifies Over Athlete Bargaining Rights
dek: The Senate voted Tuesday to clear a 60-vote filibuster threshold on the Protect College Sports Act, a bipartisan bill that would cap athlete NIL payments, restore NCAA enforcement power, and restrict transfer portal movement. The bill now heads toward a final floor vote amid competing campaigns from pro-bill coaches and White House boosters against labor unions, civil rights groups, and Democratic senators who argue it strips collective bargaining rights from athletes.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Senate voted 74-24 on September 15 to advance the Protect College Sports Act toward a final floor vote, clearing the 60-vote threshold needed to halt debate.
bottom_line: Senate votes 74-24 to advance Protect College Sports Act toward final floor vote; intense lobbying underway over NIL and NCAA power restoration.
body:
The Senate voted 74-24 on Tuesday, September 15, to advance the Protect College Sports Act toward a final floor vote, clearing the 60-vote threshold needed to halt a filibuster. With two senators absent, the vote marked a bipartisan milestone for legislation that would restore NCAA authority, cap athlete compensation, and restrict player movement, but it also crystallized a deep split over whether the bill protects athletes or exploits them.
The bill would establish a 22% cap (roughly $21.5 million this year) on revenue colleges may share with athletes, add a $27.5 million retention pool for schools to retain current players, restrict players to one free transfer without a year sitting out, and codify the NCAA's five-year eligibility rule into federal law. A second section would allow conferences to pool media rights, potentially generating $4 billion to $8 billion in additional revenue, though the SEC and Big Ten have stated they would not participate in such pooling. The bill also includes a third section funding broadband at historically Black colleges and universities.
Support from prominent coaches has driven a $10 million advertising campaign. Nick Saban and Deion Sanders have appeared in ads funded by Saving College Sports, an organization led by Texas Tech booster Cody Campbell, neither paid for the spots, per Front Office Sports reporting. Arkansas coach John Calipari said at a Monday news conference in Washington that the bill addresses roughly 75 to 80 percent of college sports issues. The White House college sports committee, which includes Campbell and New York Yankees president Randy Levine, has been central to the bill's lobbying push. Co-sponsors Senators Ted Cruz of Texas, Maria Cantwell of Washington, and Eric Schmitt of Missouri have worked to secure votes since Congress returned from recess.
Opposition has intensified across multiple coalitions. All four Black Democrats in the Senate, Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Lisa Blunt Rochester, and Angela Alsobrooks, voted against advancing the bill. Labor groups including the AFL-CIO and SEIU, and civil rights organizations including the NAACP, have begun deploying their lobbying power against the legislation. Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut has led public opposition, arguing the bill protects a system of exploitation at its core.
Athletes themselves have registered concerns. Maryland women's basketball player Oluchi Okananwa, LSU women's basketball player Jada Williams, and Temple football player Jackson Pruitt told Front Office Sports they support rules and regulation but wanted to participate in rule-making through collective bargaining. Marty McNair, father of late Maryland football player Jordan McNair, who died from heat stroke during a 2018 practice, raised concerns about loopholes in health and safety standards and prohibitions on players suing schools. NAACP CEO Derrick Johnson appeared on SportsCenter on Tuesday and stated the bill takes away athletes' rights and creates opportunity for sports leagues to commit illegal acts through antitrust exemption. Johnson characterized the HBCU funding provision as tokenizing and argued that federal law supersedes state law on collective bargaining, positioning athletes' right to collectively bargain as a centerpiece of opposition.
A Democratic Senate aide told Front Office Sports that opposition to the bill is growing among important stakeholders. The bill was introduced in late May by Cantwell and Cruz. Senator Schmitt said the bill could define the trajectory of college athletics and that there is one window to pass it before the election. Senator Cantwell told ESPN she is cautiously optimistic the bill could clear the House, which has failed repeatedly to pass a different version of college sports legislation.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority.
The Bottom Line: The final floor vote will test whether bipartisan backing can hold against growing opposition from labor, civil rights, and Democratic ranks. The SEC and Big Ten's refusal to participate in media pooling, a revenue linchpin in the bill's projections, may surface as a critical vulnerability during debate.
